analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent Inspector General to police misconduct across the federal courts, including the Supreme Court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up an Inspector General for the federal court system, modeled on the watchdogs that already oversee federal agencies. That office would investigate judicial misconduct, including violations of the newly adopted Code of Conduct for Supreme Court justices, with subpoena power and the ability to refer criminal matters to the Attorney General. It would also protect court employees who report problems from being fired or demoted. The bill received no action after its referral to the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Litigants and members of the public who depend on federal judges acting ethically. Court employees gain protected channels for reporting misconduct. Congress gains a professional fact-finder to support oversight of a branch that currently polices itself, and the Judiciary Committee gains investigative support it otherwise lacks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court users and federal court employees

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Inspector General for the judicial branch with authority to investigate alleged misconduct and violations of the Code of Conduct for Supreme Court justices [S2].

Gives the Inspector General subpoena power over testimony and records, including records held by the Judicial Conference and the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, and requires referral to the Attorney General of suspected federal crimes [S2].

Bars courts from firing, demoting, or otherwise retaliating against employees who report misconduct or possible violations of law to the Inspector General, and lets injured employees sue for relief [S2].
Excludes investigation of the merits of judicial decisions or rulings and removes any power to discipline judges, limiting the office to waste, fraud, and ethics matters rather than rulings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal judiciary, which would lose its monopoly on investigating its own members' conduct and would face a standing outside auditor. The bill also requires appropriations to fund the new office, a cost borne by taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The Inspector General would be appointed by and removable at will by the Chief Justice, the very head of the branch being policed, which raises the question of whether the office could truly act independently [S2].

Defenders of judicial independence argue that an external watchdog could chill decision-making or be used for political harassment of judges, even with the bill's limits on reviewing case merits or disciplining judges [S2].
The office would need annual appropriations, adding a new taxpayer-funded bureaucracy to oversee the courts [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real gap: the federal judiciary, including the Supreme Court after it adopted its first ethics code in 2023, investigates complaints about its own members and has no outside auditor. The main honest tradeoff is design, not cost: because the Chief Justice appoints and can remove the Inspector General, the watchdog's teeth depend on that person's independence. Still, an office with subpoena power and criminal referral duties is substantially more accountability than the current self-policing system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: The Judicial Ethics Enforcement Act of 2024 was introduced on April 19, 2024, by Rep. Melanie Stansbury with 10 original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].
The bill drew 15 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The complete action history shows only two entries: introduction and the committee referral. No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal judiciary is better off because the bill died: it keeps its current system of investigating judges' conduct internally, with no outside Inspector General, no subpoenas from an external office, and no dedicated whistleblower protections for court staff. The 15 Democratic cosponsors gained nothing; the bill left no record beyond its referral.

for.name: Rep. Melanie Stansbury
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an Inspector General for the judicial branch and recruited 10 original cosponsors

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill after it was referred to the committee; it received no further action for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill was referred to a Republican-controlled committee that took no action; no Republican sponsored it.

industries.industry: The federal judiciary, including the Supreme Court
industries.note: The bill would take away the courts' exclusive control over investigating judicial misconduct, subjecting the branch to an outside Inspector General with subpoena power. Judicial resistance to external oversight was the obstacle the bill faced, and the bill's death preserves the self-policing status quo.

industries.industry: Well-connected litigants and gift-givers with interests before the courts
industries.note: An Inspector General empowered to investigate Supreme Court ethics violations would increase scrutiny of undisclosed gifts, travel, and conflicts involving people with business before the Court. Those parties lose a measure of the discretion they currently enjoy.
